issues.subcategory: Missing random effects structure
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the mixed model includes only a random intercept for subjects but no random intercept or slope for items (suffixes or nonwords). Given that stimuli vary systematically in their properties and multiple nonwords share the same suffix, failing to account for item-level variance risks inflated Type I error rates. This is a well-known issue in psycholinguistic research (Clark, 1973; Barr et al., 2013). The same concern applies to Experiment 2, which also only includes a random intercept for subjects.
issues.quote: We included a random intercept for subjects. This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent test statistics across text and table
issues.description: For the regressions-out measure in Experiment 3, the text reports B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25, z = 2.65, p < 0.01. These values are inconsistent for what should be the same analysis. The estimate differs (0.3 vs 0.25) and the z-value differs (3.12 vs 2.65).
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent go-past time estimates
issues.description: For go-past time, the text reports B = 41, t = 3.837, but Table 5 reports B = 43, t = 3.76. The mean difference reported in the text is 49 ms (458 vs 507) but the estimates are 41 or 43, suggesting additional covariates are absorbing variance, but the two reported estimates should at least be internally consistent.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: Missing power analysis
issues.description: No power analyses or sample size justifications are provided for any of the three experiments (N=46, N=29, N=47). Given that some of the key effects are graded (diagnosticity/specificity modulating congruency effects), it is unclear whether these sample sizes provide adequate power, particularly for the interaction effects and the separate analyses of adjective- vs noun-diagnostic suffixes in Experiment 1.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory directional predictions for diagnosticity vs specificity
issues.description: The authors predict that diagnosticity (spelling-to-meaning) should impact tasks requiring access to grammatical information from print (Experiments 1 and 3), while specificity (meaning-to-spelling) should impact spelling production (Experiment 2). However, they label this as 'feedforward' effects, which is confusing because diagnosticity describes the forward mapping from spelling to meaning, yet they also state 'we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning.' This appears to reverse the predicted direction: diagnosticity should logically affect reading (print-to-meaning), not spelling production, and specificity should affect spelling (meaning-to-print), not reading. The actual experiments seem to test the correct mapping (diagnosticity for reading/classification, specificity for spelling), contradicting this stated prediction.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning

issues.subcategory: Unbalanced number of words pre-target across conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the number of words before the target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs 5.23, p < 0.05). This means that the amount of contextual information available before encountering the target nonword differs across conditions, which could confound the congruency effect. More pre-target words in the incongruent condition could provide stronger syntactic expectations, amplifying the congruency effect.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Missing details on random effects for Experiment 3
issues.description: For Experiment 3, the authors state models included 'random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' but do not include random intercepts for items (individual nonwords). Since each suffix appears with four different stems, there is item-level variability not captured by suffix-level random effects. Additionally, no random slopes are included, which may lead to anti-conservative inference (Barr et al., 2013).
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: High rate of missing data in Experiment 1
issues.description: 11.7% of data points were missing in Experiment 1 due to timeouts or non-responses. This is a substantial proportion. No analysis is provided to determine whether missingness was systematic (e.g., related to suffix type, diagnosticity level, or participant characteristics), which could bias the results.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.subcategory: Inclusion of pseudoaffixed words in corpus analysis
issues.description: The computational analysis deliberately includes pseudoaffixed words (e.g., 'corner' for -ER) alongside genuinely suffixed words. While the authors justify this by citing evidence that readers identify morphemes in pseudoaffixed words, this conflates the linguistic construct (actual morphological structure) with the psychological construct (perceived morphological structure). The diagnosticity and specificity values are therefore a hybrid measure that may not accurately reflect either the true morphological structure of English or readers' perceptions.
issues.quote: We included pseudoaffixed words because there is evidence that people identify morphemes within these (Rastle, Davis, & New, 2004).

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc selection of eye-tracking measures
issues.description: The authors acknowledge having no concrete predictions about which eye-movement measures would show effects, and chose to monitor a variety of measures. This creates a multiple comparisons problem: six dependent variables were tested, increasing the family-wise error rate. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied, and the significant results on go-past time and regressions-out could be inflated by this analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of token-based analyses
issues.description: For Experiment 2, the token-based analysis of the specificity × condition interaction is reported only as 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01'. A z-value of 0.60 would correspond to p ≈ 0.55, not p < 0.01. This appears to be either a reporting error or the z-value is incorrect.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.subcategory: Implausible z-value and p-value combination
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the token analysis reports z = 0.60 with p < 0.01. A z-value of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.549, which is far from significant. Either the z-value or the p-value must be incorrect.
issues.quote: for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01

issues.subcategory: Sample restricted to university students
issues.description: All three experiments use undergraduate students from a single university (Royal Holloway, University of London). The authors make broad claims about 'skilled readers' and 'the average reader' but the sample is restricted to young, highly educated adults at a UK university. This limits generalizability to the broader population of skilled readers.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from correlational corpus data
issues.description: The authors argue that 'the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional' and that 'English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information.' This is a strong functional/teleological claim that cannot be supported by the correlational evidence presented. The observed patterns could be epiphenomenal rather than functional.
issues.quote: the proliferation of spellings in English may actually be functional... English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information

issues.subcategory: No counterbalancing of suffix-to-context assignment in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, each participant saw all 66 sentences with the same assignment of suffixes to congruent/incongruent contexts. There is no counterbalancing such that each suffix appears in both congruent and incongruent conditions across participants. This means that any idiosyncratic properties of specific nonword-sentence pairings are confounded with the congruency manipulation.
issues.quote: Each subject saw all 66 sentences.

issues.subcategory: Comprehension accuracy reported as percentage not proportion
issues.description: Average accuracy on comprehension trials is reported as '0.86%' which should presumably be 86% or 0.86 (proportion). The '%' symbol makes this ambiguous and potentially misleading, suggesting near-zero accuracy.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: Verb fillers not analyzed but contribute to task demands
issues.description: In Experiment 3, 40 filler nonwords with verb-diagnostic suffixes were included but not analyzed because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' However, these fillers constitute one-third of the trials and could influence participants' strategies and expectations. The decision to exclude them from analysis is not well justified given that they were included to balance contexts.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be balanced across all three lexical categories. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category

issues.subcategory: Lexical category as proxy for meaning
issues.description: The paper frames its investigation as studying the relationship between 'spelling and meaning' but operationalizes meaning exclusively as lexical category (noun, adjective, verb). Lexical category is only one aspect of meaning, and the title and abstract's framing of 'meaningful regularities' may overstate what is actually being measured. The authors acknowledge this briefly but the framing throughout the paper is broader than the operationalization.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of "meaning").

issues.subcategory: Sign transformation of diagnosticity variable
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the authors multiplied diagnosticity by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes to create a single continuous predictor. This transformation assumes a linear relationship and imposes a specific functional form. The authors acknowledge this concern by running separate analyses, but the primary analysis uses this transformed variable, which could introduce artifacts.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Missing degrees of freedom and confidence intervals
issues.description: Throughout the experiments, the authors report B values, z/t values, and p-values but never report confidence intervals, effect sizes (e.g., odds ratios for logistic models), or degrees of freedom for t-tests in the linear mixed models. This makes it difficult to evaluate the precision and practical significance of the effects.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 conducted after unrelated testing session
issues.description: Experiment 1 was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session. Participant fatigue could affect performance, and the nature of the preceding task could prime or interfere with lexical category judgments. No information is provided about the preceding task or its potential influence.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistency in number of suffixes after exclusion
issues.description: The computational analysis identifies 154 suffixes, then excludes those occurring in fewer than 20 words (64 suffixes). The text states 'For the remaining 95 suffixes' but 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. This arithmetic discrepancy suggests either the exclusion criterion or the count is incorrect.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes... For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.subcategory: Entropy analysis interpretation
issues.description: The entropy analysis comparing Hspelling and Hsound finds a slope of 0.9 that is significantly different from 1. However, the mean entropy values are very close (0.61 vs 0.63), and the practical significance of this difference is unclear. The authors interpret this as evidence that spelling is 'more predictive' of category than phonology, but the effect is very small and the regression approach (predicting Hspelling from Hsound) tests a different hypothesis than a direct comparison of predictive power.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration mentioned
issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for any of the three experiments. Given the multiple dependent variables in Experiment 3, the exploratory nature of some analyses (e.g., separate analyses for adjective vs noun suffixes in Experiment 1), and the various ways diagnosticity/specificity could be operationalized (type vs token), pre-registration would have been valuable for distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: Data for all experiments can be found in the OSF storage for this project.

issues.subcategory: Potential confound of suffix length and frequency with diagnosticity
issues.description: The suffixes selected for the experiments vary in length, frequency, and productivity, all of which could be confounded with diagnosticity and specificity. No analysis is reported controlling for these potential confounds in the behavioral experiments. For example, longer suffixes may be more recognizable and also more diagnostic, creating a confound.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected (See Table 2). These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.subcategory: Missing information about list assignment in Experiment 1
issues.description: In Experiment 1, stimuli were divided into two lists of 40 items, but it is not reported how many participants were assigned to each list, or whether list was included as a factor in the analysis.
issues.quote: Stimuli were divided into two experimental lists with 40 items per list. Participants saw only one list; each suffix occurred twice only.

issues.subcategory: Forced binary choice may not capture uncertainty
issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants were forced to choose between 'noun' and 'adjective' for each nonword. This binary forced-choice design does not allow participants to express uncertainty or to indicate that a nonword could be a verb or another category. This could inflate apparent sensitivity to diagnosticity by forcing responses into the two available categories.
issues.quote: participants indicated their adjective-noun decisions via button press

issues.subcategory: Diagnosticity values in Table 2 don't sum correctly
issues.description: For the suffix +an in Table 2, the type diagnosticity for nouns is listed as 0.50. However, in Appendix A, the diagnosticity values for +an are: Adjective = 0.496, Noun = 0.504, Verb = 0.000. The Table 2 value appears rounded, but the text states the threshold for inclusion was 'greater than or equal to 0.50.' The actual noun diagnosticity of 0.504 barely meets this criterion, and the adjective diagnosticity of 0.496 does not. Yet +an is included as a noun-diagnostic suffix despite having nearly equal diagnosticity for adjectives (0.496) and nouns (0.504), making it a poor exemplar of a noun-diagnostic suffix.
issues.quote: +an ... Type diagnosticity 0.50

issues.subcategory: Circularity in corpus-behavior comparison
issues.description: The authors derive diagnosticity and specificity from a corpus (CELEX), then test whether these values predict behavior, and interpret the correlation as evidence that readers have internalized writing system statistics. However, the CELEX database reflects the language that these readers have been exposed to, so finding a correlation is somewhat circular—it would be surprising if readers' behavior did not reflect the statistical properties of the language they read. A stronger test would involve manipulating diagnosticity/specificity orthogonally or using artificial languages.
issues.quote: These results suggest that skilled readers' long-term knowledge represents the statistical structure of the writing system.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 token analysis incomplete reporting
issues.description: For Experiment 2, the main effect of condition is reported for the type-based analysis, but the token-based main effect is not reported. Only the interaction with specificity is mentioned for token analyses, and as noted, with an implausible z-value.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant... (for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: No control for phonological cues in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 tests whether suffix spellings influence lexical category judgments, but the nonwords were presented visually, meaning participants could also access phonological information through subvocal reading. Since phonological cues to lexical category exist (as reviewed in the introduction), the observed effects could be driven by phonological rather than orthographic properties. The authors acknowledge this ('We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues') but this limits the interpretability of the results.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).
